newsitem.title: USA: Poland economic record drew US investors to Yankee.
newsitem.headline: Poland economic record drew US investors to Yankee.

text.p: Poland's ability to place a $400 million debt issue on the Yankee bond market demonstrated the country's firm credit-standing and progress in implementing economic reform, U.S. investors said Thursday.
"It's a positive sign for Poland that they were able to enter the capital markets for a sizable new issue," said one U.S. portfolio manager who specializes in emerging markets.

Late Thursday, Poland placed $300 million in notes due 2004 at 75 basis points over a blend of U.S. Treasury bonds due May 2004 and August 2004, and $100 million in bonds at 100 basis points over the U.S. T-bond due July 2017.

In appealing to investors, Poland boasted a track record of five percent growth each of the past three years, declining unemployment and inflation figures, and the country's aspirations to join both the European Union and NATO.

"The focus of the distribution was on U.S. insurance companies and pension funds, investment advisors and other investment grade buyers new to Poland," said John Massad, debt syndicate desk head at JP Morgan, lead manager of the deal.

The prices may not have attracted traditional emerging market investors, but Poland's investment grade credit rating -- BBB-minus from Standard & Poor's and Baa3 from Moody's Investors Service -- meant that many U.S. institutional players could participate.
"The pricing is probably in line with other investment grade credits," one investor said.
"They priced this right around with U.S. BBB corporates."
Poland's economic record and capacity to place bonds so close to benchmark U.S. Treasuries meant that typical emerging market investors sat out the issue.

"For emerging market dedicated portfolios this is probably too low a yield to be interesting," one portfolio manager said. "It's not that Poland isn't a good credit, it's just that the yield isn't enough to get our interest."
Another positive element of the deal was that Poland would have added capital to repurchase some of its expensive Brady bonds, which are collateralized by U.S. Treasuries.
News of the pricing may have already been reflected in asset prices, as Poland's Brady bonds ended lower Thursday. Its PDIs dropped 3/4 to 85-1/2 bid, and its pars gave back 1/2 to 57-1/4.
